titulo: Simulate before you break things: sim, evaluation, and sim-to-real
lead: Testing on the real robot costs time, parts, and patience. The simulator lets you fail a thousand times for free and gives you one number: the success rate. But the number only counts if the test is hard enough and if the simulated world looks like the real one.
objetivo: evaluate a policy in simulation and know why LIBERO alone is no longer enough.

aprende.t: The 2026 simulators: MuJoCo, Isaac Sim/Lab, and Newton
Run lerobot-eval and read the success rate
Why a saturated benchmark doesn't separate models
Randomization and system identification against the reality gap

hero_alt: Monitor with a 3D simulation of an arm pushing a T-shaped block next to the real arm on the table.

secoes.titulo: From simulator to the real world

nos.detalhe: MuJoCo is at 3.16.0 (10/14/2026); since 3.5.0 (Feb/2026) it has MuJoCo Warp, built by NVIDIA and Google DeepMind to run many simulations in batches on the GPU. Isaac Sim 6.1 came out in Sep/2026; Isaac Lab 3.0 is in early access (09/16/2026) and has no final release yet.
A fixed set of tasks and a success count. In LeRobot 0.6, several benchmarks run through the same lerobot-eval. LIBERO-plus and RoboTwin 2.0 are harder versions, created because LIBERO got saturated.

nos.sub: where the real score comes from

itens.t: RoboArena: A/B between policies on real robots

nos.detalhe: What works in the simulator can fail on the real robot: different friction, lighting, camera, and motor delay. RoboArena compares policies in pairs on distributed real robots and builds a ranking.

secoes.volta: Gap between sim and real? Randomize the simulator, measure the robot (sysid), and test again
secoes.legenda: Simulation to fail cheaply; benchmark to compare; real world to decide.
secoes.dica: Reality gap = the distance between what the policy sees and feels in the simulator and on the real robot.

secoes.titulo: Three ideas so you don't fool yourself

texto: In 2026 several models score above 97% on LIBERO: OpenVLA-OFT 97.1%, X-VLA 98.1%, MolmoAct 2-Think 98.1%. When everyone gets a top score, the test doesn't separate anyone.
That's why harder tests (LIBERO-plus, RoboTwin 2.0) and real-world evaluation (RoboArena, MolmoBot) are showing up.
Instead of a perfect simulator, you deliberately vary color, lighting, friction, mass, and camera position in every episode.
A policy that learns with that much variation treats the real world as just one more variation.
You measure the real robot (mass, friction, motor delay) and tune the simulator to match.
MuJoCo 3.5.0 (Feb/2026) brought a Python toolbox for this, plus actuator and sensor delays.

exemplo.texto: Use both together: measure what you can measure and randomize the rest.

{'avg_sum_reward': 19.45..., 'avg_max_reward': 0.275..., 'pc_success': 0.0, 'n_episodes': 20, 'eval_s': 14.0...}

LeRobot 0.6.1. With 200 steps: 13 s total, on both GPU and CPU only (the evaluation is light). pc_success is the success rate in %; avg_max_reward shows how close the policy got to the target (higher is better). Both short trainings give 0% success: the policy still doesn't push the T to the target, but with 5000 steps it gets closer (0.08 → 0.28).

• "Namespace gym_pusht not found": happened here with more than one environment in parallel. The --eval.use_async_envs=false option fixed it.
  • Old checkpoint from the Hub: lerobot/diffusion_pusht needs a format migration in 0.6 and doesn't run directly. Evaluate your own.
  • Reading 0% as "it doesn't work": with few steps it's expected. Look at the reward and the videos to see if it improved.
  • No display: on a server without a monitor, use SDL_VIDEODRIVER=dummy before the command.

exercicios.texto: Install lerobot[pusht] and run the lerobot-eval from the box (cpu or cuda).
exercicios.pronto: the terminal shows pc_success and n_episodes: 10, and outputs/eval/act_200/eval_info.json exists.

exercicios.texto: Open two videos in outputs/eval/act_200/videos/pusht_0/ and describe in one sentence what the policy does wrong.
exercicios.pronto: your sentence says where it fails (doesn't reach the block, pushes it the wrong way, stops midway).

exercicios.texto: If you did the 5000-step training, evaluate it too (change --policy.path and --output_dir) and compare avg_max_reward.
exercicios.pronto: you have both numbers side by side and can say which policy got closer to the target.

perguntas.p: What does pc_success in lerobot-eval measure?
opcoes: The percentage of episodes in which the policy completed the task
perguntas.explica: It's the success rate over N episodes. Loss comes from training; success comes from the task. They are different numbers.

perguntas.p: Why is LIBERO alone no longer enough to compare VLAs?
opcoes: Because it is saturated: several models score above 97%.
Because it only runs on a real robot.
perguntas.explica: With everyone near 100%, the test doesn't separate them. Use harder versions (LIBERO-plus, RoboTwin 2.0) or real-world evaluation (RoboArena).

perguntas.p: Deliberately varying lighting, friction, and mass in the simulator on every episode is…
perguntas.explica: Randomization teaches the policy to tolerate variation. System identification does the opposite: it measures the robot and tunes the simulator to match it.

perguntas.p: Your policy had 0% success and avg_max_reward went from 0.08 to 0.28 with more training. What do you conclude?
opcoes: That the policy improved, but still doesn't complete the task: it needs more training or data.
That it's ready for the robot.
perguntas.explica: Success is binary per episode; the reward shows how close it got. Short training is for learning the loop, not for solving the task.

itens.texto: Simulator to fail cheaply, benchmark to compare, real robot to decide.
lerobot-eval runs N episodes and returns pc_success and videos.
Randomize what you can't measure and measure what you can (sysid).
